chapter_theme: The sixth ten, Kakkaipadiniyar Nachchellaiyar's songs for Adukotpattu Cheralathan: a king soft-seeming at home and like Death in battle, a hand that only gives, a war elephant that would charge his own city's gate, a giver who should forgo heaven and rest like a cloud after rain, the dance motif turned three ways (the queen's anger at the thunangai, the denial of festival skill, the victory dance on the field), virali guide poems, and the king's duty to keep the roads open; the preface ties his name to seized goats and his title Vaanavaramban to a gift.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's terror in battle against his gentle look at home

51.reading: The poet tells the king that because he lingers in his cool sea-coast land, where the palmyra grove sways like a possessed girl dancing and the viralis sing to him, those who do not know him may think the lord of the white spear is gentle; but he is like the thunderbolt that strikes the angry snake on the cloud-hung hill, and his look in battle, where his spearmen cut the tusks of elephants and the drums torn by arrows fall silent, is Death spreading its net.
51.nuance: The poem turns on a mistaken impression (மெல்லியன் போன்ம், line 23): the long, lush seaside description of lines 1 to 22 is the evidence the unknowing would use, and the second half answers it with two similes of sudden killing, the thunder and Death's net. The softness is not denied; it is placed at home. Lines 12 to 16 (gems, snakes, conches, the canopy between the eastern and western seas) are compressed and their syntax is hard to fix.

comparisons.tenor: the opened neythal flowers, like eyes
the king, who strikes like the thunderbolt that kills the snake

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the hand that wins wars and only gives, then shows the king refused by his queen

52.reading: The poet says she has heard that the king's hand, which won the good war when his elephants and chariots spread into foreign land like a great ship turned from its course and his warriors reached the high world, bends only to give to suppliants and never opens to take; but now, when he came leading the thunangai dance by lamplight, giving his lead hand to others, his queen grew angry, trembling like a sprout in a flood, refused him the small red kuvalai he begged for, asked 'who are you to us?' and turned away with a hot look, so that he who is able at taking the parasol kings' forts is asked how he can be able here.
52.nuance: The colophon's குரவைநிலை names the dance, and the poem sets a domestic oodal inside a praise of war and giving: the hand that never opens to receive (lines 11, 12) is the hand that begs a flower from the queen and is refused (line 23). The closing lines are hard; they seem to play the king's strength against forts against his helplessness before her.

comparisons.tenor: the army spreading into foreign land
the queen's small feet, like an opening flower

comparisons.vehicle: ஞாயிற்(று) உருபுகிளர் வண்ணம் கொண்ட வான்தோய் வெண்குடை
comparisons.tenor: the kings' parasols, bright as the sun

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's war elephant by warning it would charge his own forts

53.reading: The poet tells the king that when the foes he camped against give tribute and he grants them grace and goes home to his ancient famous city, he should take another road and not lead his elephant past the forts his forebears guarded, with their trap-set gates, crocodile moats and sky-high walls, because, apart from the forts he won himself, his spotted-browed elephant, on seeing any gate of gold-bound planks, will brush off the goad, curl its trunk and charge with the banner waving, and none can hold it.
53.nuance: The praise is a warning against the king's own city: the elephant has broken so many gates that it cannot tell a friendly gate from an enemy's, so the hyperbole flatters the army while seeming to fear it. வேங்கை (line 18) is read as the tiger whose stripes the brow outdoes; it could also be the vengai tree, whose spotted flowers are the usual image.

comparisons.tenor: the elephant's spotted brow, outdoing the tiger's

thinai_evidence.note: the poet blesses the king on seeing him, drawn by his name as a giver

54.reading: The poet says she came to see the king because people called him a giver, wishes that he achieve what he intends and that his garland live, and since every day he scatters choice vessels without limit to end the suppliants' distress while the bright-jewelled viralis sing his valour, she wishes that he not go to the high world but abide long here on the broad earth, lord of an army that, when the drum sounds and the lancers rise with the young men, will not stand still once it sees the foes' elephants.
54.nuance: The blessing reverses the usual reward: the giver's merit would carry him to the high world, and the poet asks that he forgo it and stay where the suppliants are (lines 9 to 11). The colophon's காட்சிவாழ்த்து matches the first line: she came because of his name and blesses on seeing him.

comparisons.tenor: the viralis' rounded shoulders, like bamboo
the viralis' jewels, bright as lightning

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king who fetches suppliants and feeds them, and blesses his days

55.reading: The poet hails the king as husband of the noble queen, protector of the worthy, lord of the cool sea-garden land of fragrant thaazhai shores, shield of the Mazhavar, king of the Kudavar, who even when suppliants do not come sends chariots to bring them and gives them food, and wishes that his days, beyond the measure of years he desires, may go like the white clouds that pour rain, protect the land and rise to rest on the hill, he whose anger cooled only after he took the high-hilled lands of wailing kings.
55.nuance: The king does not wait to be asked (வாரார் ஆயினும், line 10): he fetches the suppliants. The blessing takes the rain cloud not as the model of giving but of a life that rests after giving, the cloud going up to the hill when its work is done. Lines 7 and 8 (the white pulse mash without red meat, the white meat as provision) read as the food of the Mazhavar warriors, whose shield he is.

comparisons.tenor: the king's days passing after his giving

thinai_evidence.note: the king's victory dance on the field where hostile kings died

56.reading: The poet says the king is no skilled dancer before the drums of the dancers in the wide festival ground, long live his garland, but when the victory drum sounds, with sword raised, shining ornaments and a golden uzhinai garland, he is the king who dances on the battlefield where the kings who attacked him in their great folly lose their lives.
56.nuance: A mock dispraise: the denial of skill at the festival sets up the dance that counts, the victory dance with the bright sword that the colophon's ஒள்வாள் அமலை names. The uzhinai garland (line 5) is the siege flower, so the field he dances on is one where he took forts.

thinai_evidence.note: a guide poem sending the virali to the generous king

57.reading: The speaker urges the small-bangled virali, walking on soft paths on her small feet, to tune the paalai mode on the bards' great lute, sing the thazhinji, and come with her, for they shall go to see the victorious king who danced the thunangai on the reeking battlefield where blood reddens his anklet and palmyra garland, husband of the restrained and wise queen who bore young sons, who fears the distress of suppliants more than the sulking eyes of bright-browed women and welcomes those who come for his support.
57.nuance: The opening formula செல்லா மோதில் (line 6) is read here as செல்லாமோ தில், 'shall we not go', the same words that open Purananuru 64. The king's anxiety is ranked: the suppliant's sad face is a greater fear to him than the oodal of the women of his house (lines 13, 14).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king as lord of vow-bound warriors and of a farming land

58.reading: Let the viralis dance and the gift-seekers sing, says the poet: the great lord of the warriors, who wear kuvalai on white palm leaf and bear sword scars and swore that if they feast today they will not eat tomorrow until they cross the earthen fort wall, the truthful-tongued, fort-breaking archer, shield of the worthy, is called Vaanavaramban, lord of a wide land where on dry ground under the small-leaved velam the farmers yoke their oxen and the ploughshare turns up bright gems.
58.nuance: The vow (lines 5 to 7) belongs to the warriors, not the king, and binds their next meal to the taking of the wall. The poem ends on a plough that turns up gems in poor dry land, so the warlike king is finally praised as lord of farmers.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's giving and a statement of his duty to the land

59.reading: As in the cold month of Maasi, when the night is long, the sun rises in the east and spreads its rays to end the darkness and gladden the bard crossing the cold wastes, so the king makes the small homes of suppliants grow; the poet asks whether his anger will cool if foes who opposed him without knowing his refuge bow and pay tribute, and tells him that it is his duty too to protect the land where goods of hill and sea are shared out and the roads are kept unblocked in the way of dharma.
59.nuance: The last lines (16 to 19) turn praise into a statement of duty (கடனே): keeping the roads open so the goods of hill and sea can be exchanged is named as the king's charge, beside his giving. The simile is timed: the sun of the long Maasi night is the one most longed for, as the bard on the cold road longs for the patron.

comparisons.tenor: the king, whose rising makes the suppliants' homes grow

thinai_evidence.note: a guide poem sending the bard woman to the king who wars and gives

60.reading: The speaker asks the bard woman whether they shall not go to see the king, whose army is set on killing and who is himself set on war yet gives without ceasing, where sweet fruit that bees swarm over and ripe fruit with honeyed pulp end the weariness of travellers, the harvest never fails, and warriors with unstrung bows live by the sea whose spray mingles with the mist and whose wind brings cold.
60.nuance: The first line sets the king's killing and his giving side by side without joining them. The last line (துவ்வா நறவின் சாயினத் தானே) may name the place where he stays, perhaps the Chera port Naravu, or speak of toddy; the reading is open.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's deeds, gifts and protection

patikam:6.reading: The decade's preface says that Adukotpattu Cheralathan, son of Kudakko Nedunjeralathan by the queen born of the Vel Avi line, brought to Thondi the goats seized in Dandaranya and had them given, gave the Brahmins tawny cows and a village in Kudanadu, made the name Vaanavaramban shine, crushed the other Mazhavar in war, drove off kings, protected his people as one tends an infant, and had a just heart, and that Kakkaipadiniyar Nachchellaiyar sang this ten.
patikam:6.nuance: The preface ties the king's name to a seizure of goats (வருடை, line 3; ஆடு கோள்), while the songs play on ஆடு as dance (52, 56, 57); the two explanations sit side by side in the same decade. The title Vaanavaramban, which 58 gives him in the songs, is here earned by a gift.

comparisons.tenor: the king protecting his people, as nurses tend an infant

links.note: Kural 222 says taking is bad even if called a good path, and giving good even without a higher world; Patitruppattu 52 says the king's hand bends down to give to suppliants and does not know how to open upward to take (இரப்போர்க்குக் கவிதல் அல்லதை இரைஇய மலர்பு அறியா).
links.teaches: The poem turns the couplet's two verbs into two postures of one hand, palm down to give and palm up to receive, so the rule against taking becomes a bodily habit the king cannot break.

links.note: In Purananuru 98 the foes who see Anji's war elephants with blunted tusks bar their fort gates; Patitruppattu 53 warns the Chera to take another road home, since his elephant, seeing any gate, will charge it.
links.teaches: Read together they show the praise of the war elephant pushed one step further: in Avvai's poem the gates close in fear, while the Chera poet makes the elephant's habit so fixed that the king's own ancestral city is in danger, so the boast works by turning the threat inward.

links.note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; Patitruppattu 54 wishes that the giving king not go to the high world (உயர்நிலை உலகத்துச் செல்லாது) but stay long on the earth.
links.teaches: The couplet sets heaven aside as irrelevant to the worth of giving, while the bard treats the giver's heaven as a loss to those who live on his gifts and wishes it postponed, so the same detachment of giving from heaven appears once as an ethic and once as the suppliants' self-interest.

links.note: Kural 211 asks what the world gives back to the rain, to show that obligation seeks no return; Patitruppattu 55 wishes the giving king's days to pass like white clouds that pour rain, protect the land and go up to rest on the hill.
links.teaches: Both use the rain cloud for the giver, but the Kural stops at the absence of return, while the Chera poem imagines what the cloud has after giving, rest on the hill, and makes that the blessing on the king's lifespan.

links.note: Patitruppattu 56 says the king is not skilled at dancing before the drums of the festival ground (ஆடல் வல்லான் அல்லன்); 52, in the same decade, shows him leading the thunangai dance by lamplight, giving his lead hand, until the queen grows angry.
links.teaches: On a literal reading the two poems disagree about whether he dances at festivals, and holding them together shows that 56's denial is a joke the decade's hearers would see through, a mock dispraise that only works because his festival dancing was known.

links.note: Both are virali-guide poems that open with the same words, செல்லா மோதில் சில்வளை விறலி, and send the dancing woman to a king on the battlefield; Purananuru 64 says they will see Kudumi and leave behind their watery gruel, Patitruppattu 57 says they will see the king who fears suppliants' distress more than women's sulking eyes.
links.teaches: The shared formula shows that the virali guide poem had a fixed opening used across Pandya and Chera praise, and the difference in what follows shifts the motive from the bard's hunger in the Purananuru to the patron's own anxiety in the Patitruppattu.

links.note: Kural 224 says being begged from is painful until one sees the asker's glad face; Patitruppattu 57 says the king fears the distress of suppliants more than the sulking eyes of the women of his house (ஒண்நுதல் மகளிர் துனித்த கண்ணினும் இரவலர் புன்கண் அஞ்சும்).
links.teaches: The couplet names the giver's discomfort in general, and the poem measures it against the strongest private disturbance of akam, a wife's sulk, so the giver's pain is ranked above domestic love.

links.note: Kural 120 says true trade for merchants is caring for others' goods as their own; Patitruppattu 59 tells the king that protecting the land, where goods of hill and sea are shared out and the roads stay unblocked in the way of dharma, is his duty.
links.teaches: The Kural places fair trade in the merchant's conscience, while the Chera poem names the condition it assumes, open roads that the king must keep, so the trader's ethic depends on a ruler's duty the couplet does not mention.

source_issues: 51-60: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); the patikam has neither thinai nor thurai. All are marked paadaan here except 56 (vaakai, by its ஒள்வாள் அமலை victory dance).
தாணஇயர் (52 lines 3 and 28, 53 line 1, 58 line 4) and தாணஇப் (53 line 15) look like unrepaired TSCII leftovers for தரீஇயர் / தரீஇ; they are not flagged.
55 line 10: வேணடித் is a misprint for வேண்டித்.
51 line 14 and 55 line 3: பெளவத்து is written with ெ + ள rather than ௌ (பௌவத்து); an encoding variant.
57 line 6 and 60 line 3: செல்லா மோதில் is spaced as two words that should be read செல்லாமோ தில், as Purananuru 64 line 2 has it.
53 spells the thurai செந்துறைப் பாடாண்பாட்டு with a space; 55, 58 and 59 write செந்துறைப்பாடாண்பாட்டு without.
Repeated lines flagged: 58 lines 3 and 19 (with 67 and 66), 59 line 12 (with 62), patikam:6 lines 10 and 14; repaired TSCII lines flagged in 51 (2, 36), 53 (9), 59 (16), 60 (4, 10) read plausibly.
patikam:6 line 14 is the prose colophon kept as a verse line.
